company.name: Meridian Software
company.description: B2B SaaS, ~90 people, sells a workflow analytics product to mid-market and enterprise customers. The flagship release this period is Orion, a rebuilt reporting and onboarding experience.
company.note_on_inherited_transcripts: Four transcripts already exist in data/ (sample_transcript, meeting_week1, meeting_week2, meeting_week3) and stay in the corpus. They are the launch standups of 2025-04-14, 04-21, 04-28 and 05-05. They contain day-of-week/date slips (e.g. 'Wednesday, May 1' when May 1 2025 is a Thursday) and disagree with each other about whether the beta date was April 28 or May 1. Both are kept, not corrected: they are realistic transcription artefacts and one of them is a deliberate inconsistency thread. They also literally write 'Decision:' and 'Action item:' as line prefixes, which is the one thing generated meetings must NOT copy. See speech_style.how_decisions_surface.

cast.name: Alice
cast.role: VP Product. Chairs standups and all-hands. Owns the launch decision.
cast.style: Opens with a short personal beat then drives hard to a decision. Always asks for an owner and a date. Uses 'let's park that', 'circle back', 'I don't want to guess today'. Cuts off circular discussion.

cast.name: Bob
cast.role: Staff engineer, platform and backend. Owns rate limits, capacity, feature flags.
cast.style: Hedges with numbers he half-remembers. 'honestly', 'hang on—', 'two more sprints, realistically'. Interrupts himself mid-sentence. Volunteers feature flags as the answer to everything. Pessimistic about launch week.
cast.concentration: Orion and platform. Rarely in Atlas reviews.

cast.name: Sarah
cast.role: Design lead. Owns flows, copy freeze, and raised accessibility first.
cast.style: Careful not to overpromise. 'I don't want to overpromise on timing', 'that works as long as—'. Raises compliance and accessibility even when nobody asked. Trails off when unsure.
cast.concentration: Orion and accessibility. Never in Atlas or finance meetings.

cast.name: Marcus
cast.role: Legal counsel. Owns vendor contracts, TOS, DataCorp escalation.
cast.style: Formal and slightly stiff. Counts things in business days. 'I'd want that in writing', 'I can't commit to that timeline'. Describes process before conclusions. Rarely gives a hard date.
cast.concentration: HEAVILY CONCENTRATED on datacorp_contract and legal sign-off. Absent from Atlas reviews, telemetry, capacity and most of July and August.

cast.name: Priya
cast.role: Engineering manager. Joined to run delivery across Orion and Atlas.
cast.style: Terse. Refers to tickets by number ('ORI-412'). 'Who's blocked?', 'that's two sprints, not one'. Impatient with status without a decision. Pushes back on scope openly.
cast.concentration: Delivery across both projects, but only from April onwards. Completely absent from March.

cast.name: Danny
cast.role: QA lead. Owns test passes, smoke tests, audit verification.
cast.style: Dry and self-deprecating. 'I ran it twice and got two different answers.' Flags flaky tests nobody wants to hear about. Understates severity then turns out to be right.
cast.concentration: HEAVILY CONCENTRATED on accessibility_audit verification and test passes. Absent from finance, contract and Atlas discussions.

cast.name: Elena
cast.role: Finance and BizOps. Owns budget approval, headcount reqs, vendor spend.
cast.style: Apologetic about process she does not control. 'I can't commit a number today', 'we're still reconciling'. Speaks in quarters and approval queues. Never says no outright.
cast.concentration: HEAVILY CONCENTRATED on budget_approval, atlas_scope and hiring_freeze. Never attends an Orion engineering review.

cast.name: Tomas
cast.role: Customer success lead. Owns Ridgeline and the enterprise pipeline.
cast.style: Brings customer anecdotes and account names as evidence. 'Ridgeline are asking again.' Emotive about churn risk. Quotes customers verbatim.
cast.concentration: HEAVILY CONCENTRATED on ridgeline. Appears in roughly a third of meetings and almost always talks about customers. Absent from Atlas, budget and capacity discussions entirely.

cast.name: Nina
cast.role: Data and analytics. Owns activation metrics and instrumentation.
cast.style: Qualifies every number. 'directionally right', 'I wouldn't put that in a board deck yet'. Points out instrumentation gaps that make questions unanswerable.
cast.concentration: HEAVILY CONCENTRATED on rate_limits, the telemetry rebuild and activation metrics. Never in a legal, contract or Atlas meeting.

cast.name: Raj
cast.role: CTO and exec sponsor. Attends all-hands and escalations only.
cast.style: Big-picture and brief. Asks one sharp question that reframes the discussion, then leaves. Rounds numbers. Occasionally contradicts a detail the team stated precisely.
cast.concentration: MOST CONCENTRATED OF ALL. Six all-hands out of forty-five meetings, nothing else. Speaks maybe four times per all-hands.

speech_style.general: These are real spoken transcripts, not minutes and not prose. Sentences break off. People talk over each other, answer a question two turns after it was asked, and drift into tangents that go nowhere. Filler ('yeah', 'I mean', 'sort of', 'right?') appears but is not in every turn. Turns vary from three words to sixty. Not every meeting reaches a conclusion.
avoid: Clean, well-formed, self-contained sentences in every turn
Every speaker restating the full name of a project or issue each time
Summary-style turns that recap what was just said
Every meeting ending with a tidy decision and action items

turn_rhythm.requirement: MANDATORY. Real meetings are lopsided and uneven. A transcript where speakers alternate in a fixed rotation and every turn is the same length is the clearest tell that it was written rather than transcribed.
rules: NEVER rotate through the attendees in a fixed order. Speaker order must be irregular and unpredictable.
The same person frequently speaks two or three turns in a row, continuing their own thought or correcting themselves.
Many turns are two to six words: 'Yeah.', 'Still nothing.', 'Wait, what?', 'Same as Monday.', 'Not yet.', 'Mm.'
A few turns run forty to sixty words, when someone explains something properly or rambles.
One or two people dominate the meeting. At least one person in the room barely speaks, contributing two or three short turns in total.
Include at least three interruptions or abandoned sentences that end in a dash.
At least once, a question is answered two or three turns after it was asked, or never answered at all.
Two people occasionally talk past each other for a few turns before noticing.
Before finishing, check the speaker order. If it reads A, B, C, D, A, B, C, D then it is wrong and must be redone unevenly.

anchors.requirement: MANDATORY. This corpus is used to answer questions about what was said, so every meeting must contain specific checkable facts, not only vague references.
rules: At least eight turns per meeting must contain a concrete anchor: a named person, a specific weekday or date, a number, a ticket id (ORI-412, ATL-88), a named system, a named vendor, or a named customer.
Anchor a topic the first time it is raised in the meeting, then refer back to it with pronouns and short references afterwards.
Anchors must be consistent with the meeting date and with what the bible says has already happened. Never invent a date later than the meeting date as something that already occurred.

no_repetition.requirement: MANDATORY. A speaker's characteristic phrasing is a tic, not a refrain.
rules: Never reuse a character's catchphrase more than once in the same transcript. If Bob says 'two more sprints, realistically' once, he must not say it again in that meeting.
Never repeat the same complaint or status in near-identical words twice. If a point is restated, someone restates it differently, or with irritation that it is being restated.
Do not end the meeting by listing everything that was just discussed.
A speaker's characteristic phrasing belongs to that speaker alone. Never put one person's tic in another person's mouth.

how_decisions_surface.requirement: MANDATORY. Decisions and commitments must be buried in conversation, never announced as labelled minutes.
banned_patterns: Any turn beginning 'Decision:' — this is the single worst anti-pattern
A speaker cleanly stating a decision that nobody argued about first
how_decisions_surface.anti_pattern_note: The inherited meeting_week1.txt and meeting_week2.txt do exactly this, writing 'Decision: we are keeping May 1...' and 'Action item: I will prepare...' as literal line prefixes. They stay in the corpus because they are real history, but generated meetings must NOT copy that shape.
instead: A decision emerges out of disagreement: two people argue, a third proposes a compromise, the chair accepts it half-heartedly
Sometimes the decision is stated by the wrong person — someone who does not own it says 'so we're doing X then', and nobody corrects them
Sometimes it is only half-stated and confirmed a few turns later, or in a later meeting: 'wait, did we actually decide that?'
Commitments arrive sideways: 'I can probably get that done by Thursday', 'leave it with me', 'I'll look at it after the audit thing'
Some meetings raise a decision and fail to make it, and that failure is not commented on

referential_chains.requirement: MANDATORY. Speakers must refer back to things already discussed — earlier in the same meeting and in earlier meetings — using pronouns and deictic references rather than the full noun phrase. This is the single most important stylistic property of the corpus.
referential_chains.in_meeting: Once a topic has been named once in a meeting, later turns in that meeting should mostly refer to it as 'that', 'it', 'this', 'the same thing', or by a short alias.
referential_chains.across_meetings: Open with references to prior meetings that do not restate what happened: 'that slipped again', 'still no word', 'she's still on it', 'the thing we agreed last week', 'same as Monday', 'did that ever land?'
referential_chains.people: Refer to absent or previously-mentioned people by pronoun: 'she's still chasing it', 'he said Thursday', 'they've gone quiet again'.
examples: Marcus: Still nothing. I chased them again Friday.
Alice: Is she still on it, or did that move to Danny?
Sarah: It's the same six we talked about, I think. Maybe five now.
Priya: Did that ever get a ticket, or are we still just saying it in here?
Tomas: They asked again. Third time now.
Danny: I reran it after what he changed and it still fails.

ratio_by_meeting_type.standup: HIGHEST. Roughly one turn in three contains a reference that only resolves from earlier context. Everyone in the room shares the context and nobody bothers restating it.
ratio_by_meeting_type.project_review: MIDDLE. Roughly one turn in five. Deeper discussion needs more things named explicitly, and occasional attendees need orienting.
ratio_by_meeting_type.all_hands: LOWEST. Roughly one turn in eight. The audience is wider, so speakers recap and name things in full. This is where anchored, quotable statements concentrate.

referential_chains.balance: Each meeting still needs enough anchored statements (with real names, dates and numbers) to be answerable on its own — aim for anchors early in a topic and references afterwards.

thin_meetings.what: Slots with "thin": true have zero or one beats. They are marked thin deliberately.
thin_meetings.why: Retrieval difficulty. If every meeting is equally identifiable as being about a named thread, there are no hard negatives. A meeting that touches a thread without deciding anything is exactly the plausible-but-wrong chunk that retrieval must learn to rank below the one that matters.
content: Status repeats with no movement: 'same as last week', 'still waiting', 'no change'
Scheduling chatter: who is out, moving a meeting, a calendar clash, someone joining late
Tangents that go nowhere: a conference, a customer anecdote unrelated to anything, an office logistics complaint
Half-hearted attempts to revisit a topic that get parked again
Named threads ARE mentioned, but only in passing and without resolution
thin_meetings.do_not: Do not invent new plot in a thin meeting. No decisions, no new blockers, no dates committed. It must genuinely be a low-signal meeting.

inconsistent_fact_protocol.why: The four inconsistent facts are corpus noise by design, but a turn that states one of them must never become a golden question: the same question would have several disagreeing answer turns and correct retrieval would score as a miss.
inconsistent_fact_protocol.how: When a generated turn states one of the inconsistent facts (a specific number of audit findings, a Ridgeline contract value, a claim about which launch date was originally agreed, or a count of DataCorp follow-ups), the generator records that turn id in data/inconsistent_turns.json. scripts/build_golden_set.py excludes those turn ids from question generation.
inconsistent_fact_protocol.scope: Only turns that actually state the disputed value. A turn that mentions the audit without giving a number is not an inconsistent turn.

standup.character: Fast status round, blockers, occasional decision. Frequently repeats last week's blockers with no movement.

project_review.character: Deeper on one project. Scope arguments, estimates, descoping. Where the uncomfortable decisions get made.

all_hands.character: Rounded-up numbers, prepared updates, a Q&A section where someone asks the question nobody wanted asked. Raj asks one sharp question and leaves.
